Occurrences.Kwic: 一切語言是提婆宗，以這箇為主。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Linked Lamps Compendium: Yunmen Wenyan raises Mazu Daoyi’s formula, praises it, and invites a question; an unnamed monk asks for the Deva school and Yunmen answers by ranking him last among the ninety-six kinds.

Senses.Explanation: The Deva school is a named Chan case-formula: masters ask what it is, answer with a turning word, or invoke Mazu Daoyi’s claim that every verbal expression belongs to it. It is not a historical survey label for an externalist sect. In Baling Haojian’s case an unnamed monk asks, “What is the Deva school?” and Baling answers, “Snow heaped in a silver bowl.” Yuanwu Keqin says people commonly mistake this for an externalist school and rejects that reading outright. Other case collections preserve the exchange among Baling’s three turning words and build verses on the answer. A second recurrent deployment raises Mazu Daoyi’s declaration, “Every verbal expression is the Deva school; take this as principal.” Jieyun Ju tests the declaration with his staff. Yunmen Wenyan praises it, invites the question, then answers the unnamed monk by placing him last among the ninety-six kinds. These are live case deployments of the same named school-formula, not descriptions of two institutions. The sources license the translation “Deva school” and show how the label is wielded. They do not license replacing Baling’s or Mazu’s words with a fixed teaching, and Yuanwu expressly blocks the externalist-sect gloss.

Senses.Explanation: To take up the lineage's matter and keep it actively before an assembly. Its recurrent objects are “this matter,” the ancestral seal, the school's essentials, the Buddha teaching, an upward move, or the authoritative command; the action is performed in addresses, case comment, and face-to-face presentation rather than describing private possession. Wuwen Can says that he came two thousand leagues to reside at a monastery solely to sustain this matter, then raises the whisk and says, “Look! Look!” Yuanwu Keqin pairs carrying the school with upholding the ancestral seal and says the ancients entered deep mountains to sustain the school's essentials. Baiyu Jingsi describes Mazu Daoyi's sickbed answer as an all-out presentation for others. Zhean Jingfan criticizes how the ancients handled the seventeen hundred cases, while Feiyin Tongrong raises his staff and presents one move face to face. Jiguang Huo contrasts upholding the authoritative command and blocking the vital crossing with following the waves and setting up guest and host. The raw concordance has 1,140 substring matches in 261 allowlisted texts, including false joins across word boundaries; the semantic conclusions use only complete compound tokens.

Senses.Explanation: To bring something up and call attention to it: to prompt a person or repeatedly return a saying or matter to notice and examination. In a public exchange, an unnamed monk asks Gushan Shenyan to prompt him about the lineage matter; Gushan calls him closer and says, "This is prompting you." Hongzhi Zhengjue describes both participants in an exchange as each putting out a hand and bringing up the matter. Dahui Zonggao uses the verb both critically, for going once through an old saying and calling that freedom from words, and instructively, for bringing something up from time to time and amid walking, sitting, emotion, and responsive dealings. Wumen Huikai says many pick up Zhaozhou Congshen's answer and many bring it under examination. Foyan Qingyuan recalls receiving repeated earnest prompting from his late teacher. The Zen bend is the interpersonal and case-facing use: this ordinary act of calling attention becomes something done in the interview, received by Foyan Qingyuan from his late teacher, or repeatedly directed at a recorded saying, without naming a separate regimen.

Senses.Explanation: Lifting a physical object and taking up a saying are distinct attested acts: hands raise staffs or whisks, while speech raises a case, word, or question. To lift, pick up, or hold aloft a physical object. The exact expression occurs 1,995 times in 336 allowed files representing 331 independent works, with this concrete action repeatedly made into a visible move in public encounters. Shengguang holds up a whisk and asks what it is called. An unnamed newcomer lifts a sitting cloth and makes a circle. Nanquan Puyuan lifts the disputed cat and asks the assembly to speak. Deng Yinfeng lifts his rosary when asked his age, and an unnamed Chan visitor lifts a tea bowl when asked about ‘the other side.’ These constructions move an object bodily into view; they are distinct from instructions to take up and sustain a verbal question before attention.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to take up a saying or question
AlternateTargets: to bring a question to the fore
to hold up a saying for inquiry
SearchAliases: bring forward a topic of inquiry
Senses.Note: Discursive-attention sense. Four witnesses are stored: three distinct instructions in Zhongfeng Mingben's record and one instruction by Dufeng Benshan. They use different verbal objects but establish the same action, distinct from physical lifting; variation among saying, assigned subject, and full question does not create further senses.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names to take up a saying or question for sustained attention, not to lift or hold up a physical object. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. To take up a saying or question and keep it actively before attention. Zhongfeng Mingben repeatedly directs an assembly to do this with verbal objects: a saying without the flavor of meaning, one's assigned saying of inquiry, and the complete question ‘The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?’ His surrounding predicates require beginning with it, not moving from it, continuing forward with it, and sustaining questioning while walking or sitting. Dufeng Benshan likewise instructs listeners to take up the saying they investigate at all times. This is not bodily lifting of an object; it is the continued taking-up of a verbal subject.
